The Thomaskantor and the opera king
The year Bach became Thomaskantor in Leipzig. In London Handel stakes everything on Italian opera at the Royal Academy of Music, and in Venice the 'Red Priest' Vivaldi reigns.
Turned down by its first choice, Telemann, and its second, Graupner, the council appointed its third: Bach.
An Italian opera company founded in 1719 with capital subscribed by the nobility.
Famous for its ensemble of orphaned girls. Vivaldi taught there for many years.
Court orchestra of the Elector of Saxony
A court orchestra praised as the finest in Europe. The city where the keyboard contest between Bach and Marchand was arranged in 1717.
In 1723 an opera by Fux was staged in the open air for the coronation of Charles VI.
Frederick William I, the Soldier King
The Soldier King disbanded the court orchestra the moment he took the throne. The music-loving prince (later Frederick the Great) is learning the flute in secret.

A giant of counterpoint and a master improviser. But the pay is poor, the children are many and costly, and he is forever at odds with the town council. With theory as your weapon, overturn the verdict of 'second-rate'.
Toccata and Fugue in D minor
In Dresden, Marchand ran away from a contest with me.
Seat me at an organ and I will make a fugue of any subject you give me.
King of Italian opera in London. He has funds and fame, but temperamental singers, soaring fees and the Beggar's Opera craze of 1728 lie in wait.
On a barge on the Thames, His Majesty asked for it three times over.
In Rome I competed with Scarlatti at the keyboard — and at the organ, I won.
A violin virtuoso known as the 'Red Priest'. He gave asthma as his reason for not saying Mass. In 1725 he published a set of concertos that includes The Four Seasons.
Born in 1685, the same year as Bach and barely 130 km away, yet the two never met in their lives.
He shared the favour of London with Handel, and their rivalry was mocked as 'Tweedledum and Tweedledee'.
